subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
prompt:
Atty. Lorenzo is a commissioned notary public. He is also the lawyer of Mila and Tessa, who are both sisters of his wife. He prepares their joint complaint-affidavit and notarizes it, signing the notarial certificate as notary public. When an administrative complaint is filed against him, he argues: (1) he acted more as Mila and Tessa's lawyer than as a notary public, so the disqualification rule does not apply to him; and (2) in any case, a single notarization like this is not a ground for disbarment.

(a) Did Atty. Lorenzo violate the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice?
(b) Should he be disbarred? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. He was disqualified from notarizing the complaint-affidavit of his wife's sisters. (b) No. A single violation of the disqualification rule is not a sufficient ground for disbarment, but he may be given a lighter penalty.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice disqualifies a notary public from performing a notarial act if he is a spouse, common-law partner, ancestor, descendant, or relative by affinity or consanguinity of the principal within the fourth civil degree. Under Section 27, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court, a lawyer may be disbarred for deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, grossly immoral conduct, and other serious grounds. In Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr., the Court held that removal from the Bar should not be decreed when a less severe punishment, such as reprimand, temporary suspension, or fine, would accomplish the end desired.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Mila and Tessa are the principals, and as his wife's sisters they are his relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity, the same relationship as in Jandoquile, where the notary notarized for his wife's sister. Given the clear rule, he should have refused to notarize. His claim that he acted as their lawyer fails: he signed the notarial certificate as notary public, just as in Jandoquile, where the Court said the notary 'cannot therefore claim that he signed it as counsel.' (b) Notarizing for relatives, without more, is not deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, or grossly immoral conduct. Like Atty. Revilla, Jr., who committed a single violation, he should get a penalty lighter than disbarment. In Jandoquile, that was a reprimand and disqualification from notarial practice for three months.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Atty. Lorenzo violated Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, and being their lawyer is no excuse. But he should not be disbarred; a lighter penalty, such as a reprimand and temporary disqualification as a notary public, is enough.

keyPoints: Cites Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice (disqualification rule)
Wife's sisters are relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity, so he was disqualified
Rejects the 'I acted as their lawyer' defense because he signed the notarial certificate as notary public
A single violation is not deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, or grossly immoral conduct (Section 27, Rule 138)
Disbarment is not imposed when a less severe penalty (reprimand, temporary suspension, or fine) is enough

source.part: Resolution, discussion of the first charge (notarizing for relatives) and of why disbarment is not warranted
source.excerpt: Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice clearly disqualifies him from notarizing the complaint-affidavit, from performing the notarial act, since two of the affiants or principals are his relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity. Given the clear provision of the disqualification rule, it behooved upon Atty. Revilla, Jr. to act with prudence and refuse notarizing the document. We cannot agree with his proposition that we consider him to have acted more as counsel of the affiants, not as notary public, when he notarized the complaint-affidavit. The notarial certificate at the bottom of the complaint-affidavit shows his signature as a notary public, with a notarial commission valid until December 31, 2012. … As we said, Atty. Revilla, Jr.'s violation of the disqualification rule under Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice is not a sufficient ground to disbar him. To our mind, Atty. Revilla, Jr. did not commit any deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct or gross immoral conduct, or any other serious ground for disbarment under Section 27, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court. … we were mindful that removal from the Bar should not really be decreed when any punishment less severe such as reprimand, temporary suspension or fine would accomplish the end desired.

subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
prompt:
Rosa and Ben ask Atty. Ramos, a notary public, to notarize their joint affidavit. They are not related to him, but he personally knows both of them well. They appear before him, sign the affidavit in his presence, and take an oath. Because he knows them, Atty. Ramos does not ask for any ID. The jurat he signs does not say that he personally knows them.

(a) Was Atty. Ramos required to ask Rosa and Ben for valid ID cards?
(b) Was there anything wrong with how he notarized the affidavit? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. A notary public who personally knows the affiants need not require them to show valid ID cards. (b) Yes. He should have stated in the jurat that he personally knows Rosa and Ben.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 6, Rule II of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, a jurat is an act in which an individual, on a single occasion: (a) appears in person before the notary public and presents an instrument or document; (b) is personally known to the notary public or identified by the notary public through competent evidence of identity; (c) signs the instrument or document in the presence of the notary; and (d) takes an oath or affirmation before the notary public as to such instrument or document. In Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr., the Court held that if the notary public knows the affiants personally, he need not require them to show valid ID cards, but faulted the notary for not indicating that fact in the jurat.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Being personally known to the notary and being identified through competent evidence of identity are alternatives under the definition of a jurat. Since Atty. Ramos personally knows Rosa and Ben, he did not need their IDs, just as the Court found that Atty. Revilla, Jr. 'was justified in no longer requiring them to show valid identification cards.' (b) Like Atty. Revilla, Jr., Atty. Ramos left out of the jurat any statement that he personally knows the affiants. The Court said Atty. Revilla, Jr. 'is not without fault for failing to indicate such fact in the "jurat"' of the document.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Atty. Ramos was not required to ask for IDs because he personally knows the affiants, but he was at fault for not stating in the jurat that he personally knows them.

keyPoints: States the definition of a jurat (Section 6, Rule II, 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice)
Personal knowledge OR competent evidence of identity: either one is enough
No need for IDs when the notary personally knows the affiants
The jurat should state that the affiants are personally known to the notary
Cites Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr.

source.part: Resolution, discussion of the second charge (no ID cards required, but the jurat should have said he knows the affiants)
source.excerpt: If the notary public knows the affiants personally, he need not require them to show their valid identification cards. This rule is supported by the definition of a "jurat" under Section 6, Rule II of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice. … Atty. Revilla, Jr. knows the three affiants personally. Thus, he was justified in no longer requiring them to show valid identification cards. But Atty. Revilla, Jr. is not without fault for failing to indicate such fact in the "jurat" of the complaint-affidavit. No statement was included therein that he knows the three affiants personally.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Marites suspects her husband Ramon of having an affair. While Ramon is away, she goes to his law office, forces open his locked desk drawers, and takes private letters between Ramon and another woman, along with his diaries. She plans to present them as evidence in her petition for legal separation. Ramon objects, invoking his right to privacy. Marites argues that, as his wife, she cannot be barred from discovering proof of his infidelity. Are the letters and diaries admissible? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under Zulueta v. Court of Appeals, the letters and diaries are inadmissible.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The Constitution declares the privacy of communication and correspondence inviolable. The only exception is a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. In Zulueta, the Court held that this applies even when the person who violated it is the spouse.
suggestedAnswer.application: Marites took Ramon's private correspondence and diaries by forcing open his drawers, without his knowledge or consent. There was no court order and no public safety or order reason. Being his wife does not change this. In Zulueta, the Court said the intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity, and a person does not give up their right to privacy by marrying.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The letters and diaries are inadmissible in the legal separation case. (Note: in Cadajas v. People, 2021, the Court later described this pronouncement in Zulueta as an obiter dictum, meaning a side remark that is not a binding precedent.)

keyPoints: Privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3)
Only exceptions: lawful court order, or public safety or order as prescribed by law
Evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding
The protection applies even against one's spouse; marriage does not waive privacy
Conclusion: the evidence is inadmissible

source.part: Ruling, discussion of the inadmissibility of the documents and papers
source.excerpt: The constitutional injunction declaring "the privacy of communication and correspondence [to be] inviolable" is no less applicable simply because it is the wife (who thinks herself aggrieved by her husband's infidelity) who is the party against whom the constitutional provision is to be enforced. The only exception to the prohibition in the Constitution is if there is a "lawful order [from a] court or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law." Any violation of this provision renders the evidence obtained inadmissible "for any purpose in any proceeding." The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify any one of them in breaking the drawers and cabinets of the other and in ransacking them for any telltale evidence of marital infidelity. A person, by contracting marriage, does not shed his/her integrity or his right to privacy as an individual and the constitutional protection is ever available to him or to her.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Lito argues that the law guarantees "absolute freedom of communication between the spouses," so his wife has no right to keep her private papers from him, and he may use them as evidence against her. How did the Supreme Court in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals address the relationship between spousal privilege and the right to privacy?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The argument fails. The Court said the freedom of communication between spouses is different from forcing each spouse to share what they know with the other.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Zulueta, the Court explained that the law insures absolute freedom of communication between the spouses by making it privileged. Neither spouse may testify for or against the other without the other's consent while the marriage subsists. Neither may be examined, without the other's consent, about any communication received in confidence from the other during the marriage, save for specified exceptions.
suggestedAnswer.application: This privilege protects communications between the spouses from being disclosed. It does not give one spouse a right to take the other's private papers. The Court stressed that freedom of communication is one thing, but a compulsion for each one to share what one knows with the other is quite another. It added that this has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity each spouse owes the other.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Lito cannot rely on the spousal privilege to justify taking and using his wife's private papers. Each spouse keeps their constitutional right to privacy.

keyPoints: The law makes communication between spouses privileged to ensure freedom of communication
Spouses cannot testify for or against each other without consent while the marriage subsists (with exceptions)
Freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share what they know
This has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity
Conclusion: spousal privilege does not allow one spouse to take the other's private papers

source.part: Ruling, last paragraph before the dispositive portion
source.excerpt: The law insures absolute freedom of communication between the spouses by making it privileged. Neither husband nor wife may testify for or against the other without the consent of the affected spouse while the marriage subsists. Neither may be examined without the consent of the other as to any communication received in confidence by one from the other during the marriage, save for specified exceptions. But one thing is freedom of communication; quite another is a compulsion for each one to share what one knows with the other. And this has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity that each owes to the other.

prompt: A trial court ordered a wife not to use certain papers she took from her husband. Her lawyer later used the papers while a Supreme Court restraining order (TRO) temporarily suspended the trial court's order. In a disbarment case, the Court cleared the lawyer. The wife now argues that this disbarment ruling settled that the papers are admissible. Is she correct? Explain, based on Zulueta v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Clearing the lawyer in the disbarment case did not establish that the papers were admissible.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Zulueta, the Court explained that the lawyer (Atty. Felix, Jr.) was acquitted of violating the trial court's injunction only because, when he used the papers, the trial court's order was temporarily restrained by the Supreme Court. Once the TRO was lifted, the prohibition on using the papers became effective again.
suggestedAnswer.application: The disbarment ruling decided only whether the lawyer violated the injunction while it was suspended. The Court said that by no means did that decision establish the admissibility of the documents and papers. It amounted to no more than a declaration that the lawyer's use of the papers to obtain the husband's admission did not violate the injunctive order.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The wife is wrong. The papers remain inadmissible, and the disbarment ruling does not help her.

keyPoints: The lawyer was cleared only because a Supreme Court TRO had suspended the trial court's order at the time
The disbarment ruling only meant he did not violate the injunction
It did not establish that the papers were admissible
Once the TRO was lifted, the ban on using the papers applied again

source.part: Ruling, discussion of Martin v. Felix, Jr.
source.excerpt: Thus, the acquittal of Atty. Felix, Jr. in the administrative case amounts to no more than a declaration that his use of the documents and papers for the purpose of securing Dr. Martin's admission as to their genuiness and authenticity did not constitute a violation of the injunctive order of the trial court. By no means does the decision in that case establish the admissibility of the documents and papers in question. It cannot be overemphasized that if Atty. Felix, Jr. was acquitted of the charge of violating the writ of preliminary injunction issued by the trial court, it was only because, at the time he used the documents and papers, enforcement of the order of the trial court was temporarily restrained by this Court. The TRO issued by this Court was eventually lifted as the petition for certiorari filed by petitioner against the trial court's order was dismissed and, therefore, the prohibition against the further use of the documents and papers became effective again.

prompt: Dr. Santos runs a small dental clinic on her lot. Only patients with appointments and her staff are allowed inside. Her neighbor, with whom she has a long-running boundary dispute, installs a rotating CCTV camera on his building that covers a large part of her clinic and lot. He says the camera is for security. Dr. Santos sues to have it removed, citing Article 26(1) of the Civil Code. The neighbor argues that Article 26(1) protects only the privacy of a 'residence,' and her property is a clinic. Decide.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Dr. Santos should win. Article 26(1) of the Civil Code is not limited to residences, and the camera violates her right to privacy.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Article 26(1) of the Civil Code makes 'prying into the privacy of another's residence' and similar acts a cause of action for damages, prevention and other relief. In Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr., the Court held that this protection should not be confined to a house or residence. It may extend to places where a person has the right to exclude the public or deny them access, such as a business office where the public is excluded and only allowed persons may enter. Courts use the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test.
suggestedAnswer.application: Dr. Santos's clinic is a place where she excludes the public and admits only patients and staff, so it falls within the protection. She has a reasonable expectation of privacy there. In Hing, the Court said cameras should not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy unless the affected person consents. Using them to pry into another's residence or business office would be no different from eavesdropping. The neighbor's camera covers a large part of her property without her consent.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The camera violates Dr. Santos's right to privacy. The court may order it removed or redirected away from her property.

keyPoints: Article 26(1) of the Civil Code: prying into the privacy of another's residence, and similar acts
The protection extends beyond residences to places where one may exclude the public, like a business office
Reasonable expectation of privacy test
Cameras may not cover places with a reasonable expectation of privacy without consent
Conclusion: the camera violates her privacy and may be ordered removed

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of Article 26(1) of the Civil Code (including the Court's quotation of Arturo M. Tolentino), and of the RTC's finding that the Court upheld
source.excerpt: This does not mean, however, that only the residence is entitled to privacy, because the law covers also "similar acts." A business office is entitled to the same privacy when the public is excluded therefrom and only such individuals as are allowed to enter may come in. … Thus, an individual's right to privacy under Article 26(1) of the Civil Code should not be confined to his house or residence as it may extend to places where he has the right to exclude the public or deny them access. The phrase "prying into the privacy of another's residence," therefore, covers places, locations, or even situations which an individual considers as private. And as long as his right is recognized by society, other individuals may not infringe on his right to privacy. … The RTC, thus, considered that petitioners have a "reasonable expectation of privacy" in their property, whether they use it as a business office or as a residence and that the installation of video surveillance cameras directly facing petitioners' property or covering a significant portion thereof, without their consent, is a clear violation of their right to privacy. As we see then, the issuance of a preliminary injunction was justified.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: What is the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, as explained in Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.? How is it applied?

suggestedAnswer.answer: It is the test courts use to determine whether a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy and whether that expectation has been violated.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Hing, citing Ople v. Torres, the Court said the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy depends on a two-part test: (1) whether, by his conduct, the individual has exhibited an expectation of privacy; and (2) whether this expectation is one that society recognizes as reasonable.
suggestedAnswer.application: Customs, community norms, and practices may limit or extend a person's reasonable expectation of privacy. So the test is applied case by case, depending on the facts. In Hing, the Court agreed with the trial court that the spouses had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their property, whether used as a business office or a residence. Cameras facing their property or covering a significant part of it, without their consent, clearly violated their privacy.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The test has two parts, one subjective (did the person show an expectation of privacy) and one about society (is it reasonable), and it is decided case by case.

keyPoints: First part: by their conduct, the person exhibited an expectation of privacy
Second part: society recognizes the expectation as reasonable
Customs, community norms and practices may limit or extend it
Determined case by case, depending on the facts

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of the reasonable expectation of privacy test
source.excerpt: In ascertaining whether there is a violation of the right to privacy, courts use the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test. This test determines whether a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy and whether the expectation has been violated. In Ople v. Torres, we enunciated that "the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy depends on a two-part test: (1) whether, by his conduct, the individual has exhibited an expectation of privacy; and (2) this expectation is one that society recognizes as reasonable." Customs, community norms, and practices may, therefore, limit or extend an individual's "reasonable expectation of privacy." Hence, the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy must be determined on a case-to-case basis since it depends on the factual circumstances surrounding the case.

prompt: Spouses Reyes sue brothers Carlo and Paolo for installing surveillance cameras facing the Reyes property. The brothers answer that the cameras are on a building owned by their family corporation, not by them. They say they are mere stockholders and so are not the proper parties. The records show the corporation is family-owned and managed by the brothers' family, and the brothers let the court inspect the building and explained the camera set-up. Are the brothers proper parties? Explain, based on Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, the brothers are proper parties to the suit.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 2, Rule 3 of the Rules of Court, a real party in interest is the party who stands to be benefited or injured by the judgment. A real party defendant is one who has a correlative legal obligation to redress a wrong done to the plaintiff by reason of the defendant's act or omission. In Hing, the Court held that not being the registered owners of the building does not automatically mean the defendants did not cause the cameras to be installed.
suggestedAnswer.application: As in Hing, the corporation is family-owned and managed by the defendants' family. The defendants acted as if they were the owners: they allowed the court inside for an inspection and explained the camera set-up. In Hing, the Court found that in such circumstances the personalities of the defendants and the corporation 'seem to merge,' and that the defendants were merely using the corporate fiction as a shield.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The brothers cannot hide behind the corporation's separate personality. They are proper parties to the suit.

keyPoints: A real party defendant has a correlative legal obligation to redress the wrong done to the plaintiff
Not owning the building does not automatically mean they did not cause the cameras to be installed
Family-owned corporation managed by their family; they acted as owners (allowed inspection)
The corporate fiction cannot be used as a shield
Conclusion: they are proper parties

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of whether respondents are the proper parties
source.excerpt: In ruling that respondents are not the proper parties, the CA reasoned that since they do not own the building, they could not have installed the video surveillance cameras. Such reasoning, however, is erroneous. The fact that respondents are not the registered owners of the building does not automatically mean that they did not cause the installation of the video surveillance cameras. … He also admitted that as early as 1998 there has already been a dispute between his family and the Choachuy family concerning the boundaries of their respective properties. With these factual circumstances in mind, we believe that respondents are the proper parties to be impleaded. Moreover, although Aldo has a juridical personality separate and distinct from its stockholders, records show that it is a family-owned corporation managed by the Choachuy family. Also quite telling is the fact that respondents, notwithstanding their claim that they are not owners of the building, allowed the court to enter the compound of Aldo and conduct an ocular inspection. … Noticeably, in these instances, the personalities of respondents and Aldo seem to merge. All these taken together lead us to the inevitable conclusion that respondents are merely using the corporate fiction of Aldo as a shield to protect themselves from this suit.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Bea, a 16-year-old student, posts photos of herself at a party on Facebook. She claims the post was set so that only a few close friends could see it, but she offers no proof other than her own testimony. One of her Facebook friends, using his own account, shows the photos to a school official, who then disciplines Bea. Bea's parents file a petition for a writ of habeas data, claiming the school violated her right to informational privacy. Will the petition prosper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, the petition will not prosper because there was no proven violation of Bea's right to informational privacy.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The writ of habeas data requires a showing, at least by substantial evidence, of an actual or threatened violation of the right to privacy in life, liberty or security. In Vivares, the Court held that before a user can have an expectation of privacy in social media activity, the user must show the intention to keep certain posts private by using measures to prevent or limit access, such as the platform's privacy tools.
suggestedAnswer.application: Bea's only proof that she limited the post is her own testimony. In Vivares, the Court gave little weight to similar self-serving statements without corroboration. Also, the photos were shown by a Facebook friend who had legitimate access to them, using his own account. In Vivares, the Court said the school officials were mere recipients who did not use unlawful means, since the information was voluntarily given to them by persons with legitimate access. Any fault would lie with the friend, not the school.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Without proof that Bea placed the photos within her protected zone of privacy, she cannot claim an expectation of privacy over them. The petition should be denied.

keyPoints: Habeas data needs substantial evidence of an actual or threatened violation of privacy in life, liberty or security
The user must show the intention to keep posts private by using privacy tools
Self-serving testimony without corroboration is not enough
The school officials were mere recipients from someone with legitimate access; no unlawful means were used
Conclusion: the petition is denied

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy
source.excerpt: In sum, there can be no quibbling that the images in question, or to be more precise, the photos of minor students scantily clad, are personal in nature, likely to affect, if indiscriminately circulated, the reputation of the minors enrolled in a conservative institution. However, the records are bereft of any evidence, other than bare assertions that they utilized Facebook's privacy settings to make the photos visible only to them or to a select few. Without proof that they placed the photographs subject of this case within the ambit of their protected zone of privacy, they cannot now insist that they have an expectation of privacy with respect to the photographs in question.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: A private school is sued in a petition for a writ of habeas data over students' photos it collected. The school argues that: (a) the writ applies only to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances; and (b) the writ applies only to entities in the business of gathering, collecting or storing data, which a school is not. Rule on both arguments, based on Vivares v. St. Theresa's College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both arguments are wrong.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 1 of the Rule on the Writ of Habeas Data makes it available against an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or of a private individual or entity engaged in the gathering, collecting or storing of data or information about the aggrieved party. Section 2 allows any aggrieved party to file, and gives a separate list of who may file only for extralegal killings and enforced disappearances.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) In Vivares, the Court said that if the writ were limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, Section 2 would not have been worded that way. The Rule's annotations state that the writ can be availed of as an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy. (b) To 'engage' in something means to do or take part in it. It does not require that the activity be done as a business. What matters is that the person or entity is gathering, collecting or storing data about the aggrieved party or their family.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, and it may be issued against a school even if the school is not in the business of collecting data. (In Vivares itself, the petition was still denied on the merits, because no privacy violation was proven.)

keyPoints: Section 2: 'any aggrieved party' may file, so the writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances
Habeas data is an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy
'Engaged' means to do or take part in something, not necessarily as a business
What matters is that the respondent gathers, collects or stores data about the aggrieved party
Conclusion: both arguments fail

source.part: Our Ruling, procedural issues: the writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances (including the Court's quotation of the Rule's annotations), and the meaning of "engaged" in the gathering, collecting or storing of data
source.excerpt: Habeas data, to stress, was designed "to safeguard individual freedom from abuse in the information age." As such, it is erroneous to limit its applicability to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances only. … The writ of habeas data, however, can be availed of as an independent remedy to enforce one's right to privacy, more specifically the right to informational privacy. … Such individual or entity need not be in the business of collecting or storing data. To "engage" in something is different from undertaking a business endeavour. To "engage" means "to do or take part in something." It does not necessarily mean that the activity must be done in pursuit of a business. What matters is that the person or entity must be gathering, collecting or storing said data or information about the aggrieved party or his or her family.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: A Facebook user argues that because her post was set to 'Friends' only, it was 'very private,' so anyone who is not her Facebook friend has no right to see it. Based on Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, is a 'Friends Only' post automatically private? What setting might have produced a different result?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A post set to 'Friends' cannot easily, much less automatically, be said to be very private.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Vivares, the Court held that a user who uses a privacy tool to grant or deny access should not be denied the informational privacy right that goes with that choice. But it also held that setting a post to 'Friends' is no assurance that it cannot be viewed by people who are not the user's Facebook friends.
suggestedAnswer.application: The Court gave these reasons: Facebook is designed to make the world more open and connected; many users 'befriend' total strangers; users often have hundreds of friends; and a friend can 'share' the post or 'tag' others who are not the user's friends, which expands the audience. The Court said that if access had been limited to the uploader through the 'Only Me' setting, or to a select few through the 'Custom' setting, the result may have been different, because the intention to limit access would be clearer.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: A 'Friends Only' post is not automatically private. Using 'Only Me' or a carefully chosen 'Custom' list more clearly shows an intention to keep a post private.

keyPoints: Using privacy tools is how a user claims informational privacy online
A 'Friends' setting is no assurance that non-friends cannot see the post
Friends can share or tag, which expands the audience; users often have hundreds of friends, including strangers
'Only Me' or 'Custom' settings may have changed the result
Conclusion: 'Friends Only' is not automatically private

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy (the "Friends" setting, and the "Me Only" and "Custom" settings)
source.excerpt: It is well to emphasize at this point that setting a post's or profile detail's privacy to "Friends" is no assurance that it can no longer be viewed by another user who is not Facebook friends with the source of the content. The user's own Facebook friend can share said content or tag his or her own Facebook friend thereto, regardless of whether the user tagged by the latter is Facebook friends or not with the former. … Thus, it is suggested, that a profile, or even a post, with visibility set at "Friends Only" cannot easily, more so automatically, be said to be "very private," contrary to petitioners' argument. … Had it been proved that the access tothe pictures posted were limited to the original uploader, through the "Me Only" privacy setting, or that the user's contact list has been screened to limit access to a select few, through the "Custom" setting, the result may have been different, for in such instances, the intention to limit access to the particular post, instead of being broadcasted to the public at large or all the user's friends en masse, becomes more manifest and palpable.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Jessa, a private individual, takes screenshots of chat messages from Mark's messaging account without his knowledge, and gives them to the prosecutor. Mark is charged with a crime based on the messages. At trial, he moves to exclude them, arguing that under Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, evidence obtained in violation of the privacy of communication is inadmissible. He also cites Zulueta v. Court of Appeals. Should the motion be granted? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The constitutional exclusionary rule does not apply, because the evidence was obtained by a private individual and not by the State.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas v. People, the Court held that the Bill of Rights is meant to protect private individuals against government intrusion, so its provisions do not apply between private individuals. The rule on admissibility under Article III must affect only evidence obtained by the State through its agents. The Court called the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals a mere obiter dictum, not a binding precedent. Privacy violations between private individuals are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws. Admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence: relevance, materiality, authentication, and the exclusionary rules.
suggestedAnswer.application: Jessa is a private individual, not a police officer or other agent of the State. So Mark cannot invoke Article III, Section 3 to exclude the screenshots. His reliance on Zulueta fails because Cadajas explained that the pronouncement there was obiter: that petition was about the return of the documents, and the documents were excluded because of the trial court's injunction. Mark's remedy for any privacy violation by Jessa lies under the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, or other laws. The screenshots' admissibility will depend on the Rules on Evidence, such as proper authentication.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The motion should be denied on the constitutional ground. The evidence's admissibility is decided under the Rules on Evidence.

keyPoints: The Bill of Rights protects against the State, not against private individuals
The Article III exclusionary rule covers only evidence obtained by the State or its agents
Zulueta's statement on inadmissibility between spouses is obiter dictum
Privacy violations between private persons: Civil Code, Data Privacy Act, other laws
Admissibility: Rules on Evidence (relevance, materiality, authentication, exclusionary rules)

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (the Bill of Rights as protection against the State, and Zulueta as obiter dictum)
source.excerpt: That the Bill of Rights embodied in the Constitution is not meant to be invoked against acts of private individuals finds support in the deliberations of the Constitutional Commission. … While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. … At any rate, violation of the right to privacy between individuals is properly governed by the provisions of the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act (DPA), and other pertinent laws, while its admissibility shall be governed by the rules on relevance, materiality, authentication of documents, and the exclusionary rules under the Rules on Evidence. In this case, the photographs and conversations in the Facebook Messenger account that were obtained and used as evidence against petitioner, which he considers as fruit of the poisonous tree, were not obtained through the efforts of the police officers or any agent of the State. Rather, these were obtained by a private individual. Indeed, the rule governing the admissibility of an evidence under Article III of the Constitution must affect only those pieces of evidence obtained by the State through its agents. It is these individuals who can flex government muscles and use government resources for a possible abuse. However, where private individuals are involved, for which their relationship is governed by the New Civil Code, the admissibility of an evidence cannot be determined by the provisions of the Bill of Rights.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Paolo gave his girlfriend the password to his messaging account. Later, she logs in and copies some of his messages, which are used as evidence against him. Paolo says his account is password-protected, so he had a reasonable expectation that no one else could access it, and his right to privacy was violated. Is he correct? Explain, applying Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. By voluntarily giving his password to his girlfriend, Paolo limited his reasonable expectation of privacy as to her, so there was no violation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court applied the reasonable expectation of privacy test from Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr. It held that a person who voluntarily gives his password to another, in effect, authorizes that person to access the account. This limits his reasonable expectation of privacy as to that person.
suggestedAnswer.application: Paolo's expectation of privacy came from his account being password-protected. But he does not claim it was hacked or accessed by unauthorized means. He gave his girlfriend the password and took no steps to exclude her. As in Cadajas, his expectation of privacy as to her was limited. The Court also said that once he made the contents available to her, she had the latitude to show others what she could access. In Cadajas, this was true even though the girl was forced by her mother to open the account.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There was no violation of Paolo's right to privacy.

keyPoints: Reasonable expectation of privacy test (from Hing v. Choachuy)
A password-protected account gives an expectation of privacy
Voluntarily giving the password authorizes the other person's access
No hacking or unauthorized means were used
Conclusion: his expectation of privacy as to that person was limited; no violation

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (application of the reasonable expectation of privacy test)
source.excerpt: Here, petitioner's expectation of privacy emanates from the fact that his Facebook Messenger account is password protected, such that no one can access the same except himself. Petitioner never asserted that his Facebook Messenger account was hacked or the photos were taken from his account through unauthorized means. Rather, the photos were obtained from his account because AAA, to whom he gave his password, had access to it. Considering that he voluntarily gave his password to AAA, he, in effect, has authorized AAA to access the same. He did not even take steps to exclude AAA from gaining access to his account. Having been given authority to access his Facebook Messenger account, petitioner's reasonable expectation of privacy, in so far as AAA is concerned, had been limited. Thus, there is no violation of privacy to speak of.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: During trial, the prosecution formally offers photos taken from the accused's online account. The accused's lawyer makes no objection. After conviction, the accused argues for the first time on appeal that the photos were inadmissible because they violated his right to privacy. Can the appellate court consider the objection? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The objection was waived because it was not made when the evidence was formally offered at trial.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court said that to exclude evidence, the objection must be made at the proper time and the grounds must be specified. For documentary evidence, the objection must be made when it is formally offered. A party who fails to object on time is considered to have waived the objection, even if the evidence would have been rejected had it been challenged properly. Also, no question will be considered on appeal unless it was raised in the proceedings below.
suggestedAnswer.application: The accused did not object when the photos were formally offered. Raising the issue for the first time on appeal is barred. In Cadajas, the accused was likewise deemed to have waived his objection, and the photos taken from his Facebook Messenger account were admissible.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The objection is waived, and the photos remain admissible.

keyPoints: An objection to evidence must be made at the proper time, with the grounds specified
For documentary evidence: object when it is formally offered
Failure to object on time means waiver, even if the evidence was inadmissible by nature
Issues cannot be raised for the first time on appeal
Conclusion: the objection is waived

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (failure to object at trial, and issues raised for the first time on appeal)
source.excerpt: Basic is the rule that in order to exclude evidence, the objection to admissibility of evidence must be made at the proper time, and the grounds therefore be specified. Objection to evidence must be made at the time it is formally offered. … When a party failed to interpose a timely objection to evidence at the time they were offered in evidence, such objection shall be considered as waived. This is true even if by its nature the evidence is inadmissible and would have surely been rejected if it had been challenged at the proper time. As a complimentary principle, it is well-settled that no question will be entertained on appeal unless it has been raised in the proceedings below.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: In Cadajas v. People, how did the Court treat the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals that evidence obtained by one spouse in violation of the other's privacy is inadmissible?

choices.A: As a binding precedent that applies to all private individuals
choices.B: As a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent

choices.D: As applicable only to married couples

explanation: B is correct. The Court said the pronouncement in Zulueta is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent. One reason is that the Zulueta petition only asked for the return of the documents. Another is that the documents were declared inadmissible because of the trial court's injunction, not because of Article III, Section 3. A is wrong because the Court said it is not binding. C is wrong because the Court did not base its treatment on any conflict with the Data Privacy Act. D is wrong because the Court did not keep it as a rule for spouses; it said the statement is not a binding precedent at all.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (discussion of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals)
source.excerpt: While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. This is because the petition brought to the Court in Zulueta simply asked for the return of the documents seized by the wife and thus, pertained to the ownership of the documents therein. Moreover, documents were declared inadmissible because of the injunction order issued by the trial court and not on account of Art. III, Sec. 3 of the Constitution.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: According to Cadajas v. People, the Data Privacy Act allows the processing of data and sensitive personal information when:

source.excerpt: Sections 4 and 8 of R.A. No. 10175 both explicitly provide that the proper penalty to be imposed for child pornography committed through a computer system should be one degree higher than that provided for in R.A. No. 9775. The potential for uncontrolled proliferation of a particular piece of child pornography when uploaded in the cyberspace is incalculable. … One degree higher than the penalty of reclusion temporal is the indivisible penalty of reclusion perpetua. subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: A government agency sues several lawyers, together with a businessman, to recover allegedly ill-gotten shares of stock. The lawyers had organized the companies for their clients and, as part of their legal services, held shares as nominees. The agency offers to drop the lawyers from the case if they name the clients for whom they held the shares and turn over the deeds of assignment they executed for those clients. The lawyers refuse, invoking the attorney-client privilege. The agency argues that a client's identity is never privileged. Who is correct? Explain, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The lawyers are correct. Under the facts, the clients' identities are privileged.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court said the general rule is that a lawyer may not invoke the privilege to refuse to name a client. But there are exceptions. Client identity is privileged: (1) where there is a strong probability that revealing the name would implicate the client in the very activity for which they sought the lawyer's advice; (2) where disclosure would open the client to civil liability; and (3) where the name would furnish the only link needed to form the chain of testimony to convict the client of a crime. In short, the identity is privileged when the client's name has an independent significance, such that disclosure would reveal client confidences.
suggestedAnswer.application: The agency's conditions themselves show that the clients consulted the lawyers, as lawyers, about the corporate set-up of the companies in question, and that the lawyers prepared the deeds of assignment as part of their legal service. Naming the clients would implicate them in the very activity for which they sought advice, and would give the agency the link it needs to build its case. As in Regala, the lawyers were sued only to pressure them into naming their clients. They were being prosecuted solely for services performed as lawyers.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The clients' identities are privileged, and the lawyers may refuse to disclose them. As in Regala, they should be excluded from the case.

keyPoints: General rule: a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity
Exception: a strong probability that disclosure would implicate the client in the very activity for which advice was sought
Exception: disclosure would open the client to civil liability
Exception: the name is the only link to form the chain of testimony to convict
Summary: privileged when the name has independent significance that would reveal confidences
Conclusion: the lawyers may refuse

source.part: Ruling, Part II, exceptions to the general rule on client identity, and how they apply to the ACCRA lawyers
source.excerpt: Summarizing these exceptions, information relating to the identity of a client may fall within the ambit of the privilege when the client's name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosure would then reveal client confidences. The circumstances involving the engagement of lawyers in the case at bench, therefore, clearly reveal that the instant case falls under at least two exceptions to the general rule. First, disclosure of the alleged client's name would lead to establish said client's connection with the very fact in issue of the case, which is privileged information, because the privilege, as stated earlier, protects the subject matter or the substance (without which there would be not attorney-client relationship). … Petitioners, therefore, have a legitimate fear that identifying their clients would implicate them in the very activity for which legal advice had been sought, i.e., the alleged accumulation of ill-gotten wealth in the aforementioned corporations. Furthermore, under the third main exception, revelation of the client's name would obviously provide the necessary link for the prosecution to build its case, where none otherwise exists.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Distinguish, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan, between (a) a client who hires a lawyer for advice on how to get around the law in order to commit an illegal act, and (b) a client who thinks he may have already done something illegal and consults a lawyer about it. Is the attorney-client privilege available in each case?

suggestedAnswer.answer: In case (a), the privilege is not available. In case (b), it is available, and the client's name cannot be disclosed if disclosure would lead to evidence not yet in the prosecution's hands.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court said the privilege cannot be invoked or used as a shield for an illegal act, because it is not within the professional character of a lawyer to give advice on the commission of a crime. But where a client thinks he may have previously committed something illegal and consults his lawyer, the privilege applies, for the same policy reasons behind the privilege in general.
suggestedAnswer.application: In case (a), the client seeks help to commit a future illegal act. This falls outside the privilege, since the privilege cannot be invoked for illegal purposes. In case (b), the client seeks advice about a past act. Whether or not the act turns out to be illegal, the prosecution cannot use the lawyer-client relationship to build its case against the client. It must gather its own evidence from other sources.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There is no privilege for advice on committing a future crime. There is privilege for a client consulting about a possible past wrongdoing.

keyPoints: The privilege cannot be used as a shield for an illegal act
Advising on the commission of a crime is not within a lawyer's professional character
A client consulting about a possible past illegal act is covered
The prosecution cannot use the lawyer-client relationship to build its case
Conclusion: (a) not privileged; (b) privileged

source.part: Ruling, Part II, distinction between seeking advice for illegal purposes and consulting about a past act
source.excerpt: An important distinction must be made between a case where a client takes on the services of an attorney for illicit purposes, seeking advice about how to go around the law for the purpose of committing illegal activities and a case where a client thinks he might have previously committed something illegal and consults his attorney about it. The first case clearly does not fall within the privilege because the same cannot be invoked for purposes illegal. The second case falls within the exception because whether or not the act for which the client sought advice turns out to be illegal, his name cannot be used or disclosed if the disclosure leads to evidence, not yet in the hands of the prosecution, which might lead to possible action against him. These cases may be readily distinguished, because the privilege cannot be invoked or used as a shield for an illegal act, as in the first example; while the prosecution may not have a case against the client in the second example and cannot use the attorney client relationship to build up a case against the latter. The reason for the first rule is that it is not within the professional character of a lawyer to give advice on the commission of a crime. The reason for the second has been stated in the cases above discussed and are founded on the same policy grounds for which the attorney-client privilege, in general, exists.

prompt: Five law partners are sued together for the same acts done in the course of their legal work. The government drops one partner from the case because he supposedly promised to reveal his client's identity, but there is no proof he actually did. The other four ask for the same treatment and are refused. Was their right to equal protection violated? Explain, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Dropping one partner but not the others, without a real and substantial distinction between them, violates the equal protection clause.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court explained that the equal protection clause requires the uniform operation of legal norms, so that all persons under similar circumstances are treated the same, both in privileges conferred and liabilities imposed. To treat one person differently, there must be a classification based on substantial distinctions arising from real differences.
suggestedAnswer.application: The partners were similarly situated: all claimed their acts were done in legitimate lawyering. The only reason given for dropping one partner was his promise to name his client. As in Regala, if there is no proof that he actually revealed his client's identity, that promise cannot justify treating him differently. The Court said it is grossly unfair to exempt one similarly situated litigant from prosecution without giving the same exemption to the others.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The four partners' right to equal protection was violated.

keyPoints: Equal protection: persons in similar circumstances must be treated alike, in privileges and liabilities
A different treatment needs a substantial distinction based on real differences
The partners were similarly situated (same claim of legitimate lawyering)
No proof the dropped partner actually revealed his client
Conclusion: equal protection was violated

source.part: Ruling, Part III, equal protection (including the Court's quotation of an earlier decision on the equal protection clause)
source.excerpt: However, respondents failed to show — and absolute nothing exists in the records of the case at bar — that private respondent actually revealed the identity of his client(s) to the PCGG. … What is required under this constitutional guarantee is the uniform operation of legal norms so that all persons under similar circumstances would be accorded the same treatment both in the privileges conferred and the liabilities imposed. … The condition also constitutes a transgression by respondents Sandiganbayan and PCGG of the equal protection clause of the Constitution. It is grossly unfair to exempt one similarly situated litigant from prosecution without allowing the same exemption to the others.

prompt: According to Regala v. Sandiganbayan, how must a lawyer treat the attorney-client privilege in order to attain effective representation?

prompt: A new government regulation requires all self-employed psychologists, lawyers and doctors to register their appointment books with a tax agency. The books would list only each client's name and the date and time of each appointment, nothing about the consultation itself. The agency says the books will be examined only if a professional is suspected of underpaying taxes, so no one's privacy is harmed. Is the requirement valid? Explain, based on Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The mandatory registration of appointment books is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy of the professionals and their clients and patients.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In IBP v. Purisima, the Court held that in deciding a claim of privacy violation, a court must determine whether a person has exhibited a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether that expectation has been violated by unreasonable government intrusion. Clients and patients have a reasonable expectation of privacy when they set appointments with professionals.
suggestedAnswer.application: People may not want it known that they are consulting a professional. The Court's examples were a battered wife consulting a lawyer, and patients seeing doctors who specialize in particular conditions. Names and dates alone 'paint no picture,' but citing Disini v. Secretary of Justice, the Court said bundling together all of a person's consultations may reveal a pattern of behavior, and that pattern is protected. The agency's claim that the books would be examined only on suspicion does not save the rule. The Court said the mere chance that a person's information may be subject to the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion. The requirement also violates the confidentiality rules of these professions.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The requirement is void as an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy.

keyPoints: Test: reasonable expectation of privacy, and whether it was violated by unreasonable government intrusion
Clients and patients reasonably expect privacy when setting appointments with professionals
Names and dates together can reveal a pattern of behavior (Disini)
The mere chance of the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion
It also violates professional confidentiality rules
Conclusion: the requirement is void

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, Part IV, mandatory registration of appointment books
source.excerpt: Granted, by themselves, names and appointment dates of patients and clients paint no picture. But as Disini teaches, bundling together all the times a person consults with a professional may illustrate a general pattern of behavior, from which information about a person could be revealed, or inferences from information that should have remained private may be drawn. It is this pattern of behavior, which can be extracted from the appointment book, that a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy over and which must be protected. Respondents stress that appointment books need to be registered only and are not automatically subject to the prying eyes of the Bureau of Internal Revenue. They add that the registered appointment books may be viewed only when the self-employed professional is suspected of not paying the correct taxes. Respondents strangely made a case against their own regulation. Nonetheless, the mere chance that a person's information may be subject to the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion. Considering the risks, this information must not be readily and publicly knowable. That clients and patients may think twice about consulting with professionals, if the government can create a dossier on them based on sensitive information extracted from the appointment book, is more than just an imagined fear.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014 required self-employed professionals to: (a) submit an affidavit of their rates, manner of billing, and the factors they consider in setting fees; (b) register their books of account; (c) register their appointment books; and (d) issue a BIR-registered receipt showing a 100% discount for pro bono services. In Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, which of these requirements were upheld, and which were struck down? Why?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Registration of books of account and the pro bono receipts were upheld. The affidavit of rates and the registration of appointment books were declared void.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A valid regulation (subordinate legislation) must be germane to the purposes of the law it implements. The registration of books of account is supported by the Tax Code. The Court also held that requiring receipts is a valid measure to ascertain the correct taxes. The right to privacy under the Constitution limits government intrusion.
suggestedAnswer.application: (b) Registering books of account is germane to the Tax Code's purpose of monitoring fees and conducting tax audits, so it is valid. (d) Issuing receipts for pro bono services is a valid way to monitor tax compliance. (a) The affidavit of rates and billing serves no legitimate purpose and has no compelling need, so it goes beyond the Tax Code. The Court noted that it does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power or raise serious ethical concerns. (c) Mandatory registration of appointment books is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy and violates professional confidentiality.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Sections 2(1) and 2(2) of the regulation are void insofar as they require the affidavit and the registration of appointment books. The DOF and BIR were permanently enjoined from implementing those parts.

Pro bono receipts: valid way to monitor tax compliance
Affidavit of rates: void, beyond the Tax Code, no legitimate purpose
Appointment books: void, unconstitutional intrusion into privacy
DOF and BIR permanently enjoined from implementing the void parts

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, Parts II to IV and the dispositive portion (receipts, books of account, affidavit of rates, appointment books)
source.excerpt: In any case, respondents may validly require them to issue receipts for services rendered pro bono to monitor their tax compliance. … Thus, this Court upholds the validity of Section 2(2) of Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014, insofar as it obligates the registration of books of accounts. It finds justification in the Tax Code, and thus, is within respondents' scope of authority. … Thus, there appears no compelling need for sworn statements of the rates and manner of billing among professionals. It is irrelevant, baseless, and serves no legitimate purpose. … Nonetheless, the mere chance that a person's information may be subject to the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion. … Sections 2(1) and 2(2) of Revenue Regulation No. 4-2014, insofar as they require the submission of an affidavit indicating the rates, manner of billings and the factors that self-employed professionals consider in their service fees, and the mandatory registration of their appointment books, are declared VOID, being issued in excess of the Department of Finance's jurisdiction.

prompt: A government agency argues that a lawyer's list of client names is not privileged information, so lawyers may be required to give it to the State. Based on Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, is the agency correct? In your answer, explain how the Data Privacy Act treats privileged information.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Citing Regala v. Sandiganbayan, the Court held that a client's identity falls within the privilege in proper cases.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Attorney-client communication is privileged under Rule 130, Section 24(b) of the Rules on Evidence and Rule 138, Section 20(e) of the Rules of Court. The Code of Professional Responsibility requires lawyers to preserve client confidences. Under Regala, as a general rule a lawyer may not refuse to name a client, but the identity is privileged when the client's name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosure would reveal client confidences. The Data Privacy Act generally prohibits the processing of sensitive personal information and privileged information. Privileged information includes all forms of data that constitute privileged communication under the Rules of Court and other laws. Processing is allowed only in the cases listed in Section 13.
suggestedAnswer.application: The agency's blanket position that client names are never privileged is wrong. The Court said, 'respondents are incorrect in arguing that the client's name is not privileged information.' Requiring lawyers to give client names to the State may force them to violate their duty of confidentiality. Data that is privileged communication is also protected under the Data Privacy Act.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Client names can be privileged in proper cases, so the government cannot simply require lawyers to disclose them.

Regala: client identity is privileged when the name has independent significance
Data Privacy Act generally prohibits processing sensitive personal and privileged information
Privileged information includes data that is privileged communication under the Rules of Court
Conclusion: the agency is wrong; names can be privileged

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: In Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, what must a court determine in evaluating a claim that the government violated the right to privacy?

choices.A: Whether the government acted in good faith
choices.B: Whether the person has exhibited a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether it was violated by unreasonable government intrusion
choices.C: Whether the person suffered actual financial loss
choices.D: Whether the information was already known to at least one other person

explanation: B is correct. Quoting In re Sabio, the Court said a court must determine whether a person has exhibited a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether that expectation has been violated by unreasonable government intrusion. A is wrong because good faith is not the test. C is wrong because proof of financial loss is not required. D is wrong because the test does not ask whether someone else already knew; in the case, the professionals knew the clients' names, yet the clients still had a reasonable expectation of privacy against the State.

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, Part IV, standard for State intrusion into zones of privacy (quoting In re Sabio)
source.excerpt: In evaluating a claim for violation of the right to privacy, a court must determine whether a person has exhibited a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether that expectation has been violated by unreasonable government intrusion.

subject: Mercantile Law
prompt: In Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, which requirement of Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014 did the Court uphold as valid?

choices.A: Submission of an affidavit of rates and manner of billing
choices.B: Registration of official appointment books
choices.C: Issuance of receipts, including for services rendered pro bono
choices.D: None; the entire regulation was declared void

explanation: C is correct. The Court said the BIR may validly require professionals to issue receipts for pro bono services to monitor tax compliance, and that requiring receipts is a valid measure. A is wrong because the affidavit was declared void for going beyond the Tax Code. B is wrong because registering appointment books was declared an unconstitutional intrusion into privacy. D is wrong because the petitions were only partly granted; registration of books of account and receipts were upheld.

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, Part II, affidavits of fees and receipts for pro bono services
source.excerpt: In any case, respondents may validly require them to issue receipts for services rendered pro bono to monitor their tax compliance. … Requiring the issuance of receipts is a valid measure that the tax collector may employ to ascertain the correct amount of taxes payable by self-employed professionals.
